title: The numbers behind the turnaround
body:
## From Peak to Impairment: Mapping the Decline

The most useful number for understanding Unitika's financial position is not any figure from the current restructuring — it is ¥162.7 billion. That was the company's consolidated revenue in the fiscal year ending March 2013, the long-run peak from which everything else flows. Against that benchmark, FY3/25 revenue of ¥126.4 billion looks merely diminished. Against the FY3/29 five-year target of ¥70 billion, it looks like a company that has chosen to amputate itself into health. Whether that surgery works depends on whether the operating profit improvement is structural or cosmetic.

| Fiscal year end | Revenue (¥B) | Operating profit (¥B) | OP margin | Net income (¥B) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mar-2013 | 162.7 | n/a | n/a | 0.6 |
| Mar-2024 | 118.3 | –2.5 | –2.1% | –5.4 |
| Mar-2025 | 126.4 | +5.9 | +4.7% | –24.3 |
| Mar-2026F (guidance) | 110.0 | +9.5 | 8.6% | +20.0 |
| Mar-2029T (5y target) | 70.0 | +6.5 | 9.3% | — |

The decade-long revenue compression from ¥162.7 billion to ¥118.3 billion by FY3/24 was not a managed retreat. It was a slow bleed through commodity fiber price erosion, overcapacity in Southeast Asia, and two failed restructuring attempts — including a 2014 effort to shift production to Thailand that Unitika's own disclosures describe as "ultimately unsuccessful." The ¥5.4 billion net loss in FY3/24, combined with negative operating profit of ¥2.5 billion, made the REVIC intervention unavoidable.

## The Impairment: Clearing the Decks

The FY3/25 net loss of ¥24.3 billion looks catastrophic in isolation, but the mechanics require unpacking. The loss was almost entirely driven by a ¥37.9 billion impairment charge — a single write-down that management used to flush the carrying value of assets that had been generating losses for years. The largest component was the Emblem Asia #4 nylon film line, a large-format production facility whose economics deteriorated as Southeast Asian competitors undercut Unitika's pricing. The Okazaki polyester chip plant, along with costs from planned facility demolitions, made up the remainder.

The strategic logic of a concentrated write-down is straightforward: by writing assets to near-zero, future depreciation charges collapse. The ¥2.0 billion cost improvement in the FY3/25 OP bridge is almost entirely this effect. That is not accounting manipulation — it is the mechanical consequence of impairment — but it does mean that part of the reported operating profit improvement will not recur once the depreciation base stabilises.

Beneath the ¥37.9 billion charge, however, operating profit actually turned positive, moving from –¥2.5 billion in FY3/24 to +¥5.9 billion in FY3/25. The bridge breaks down as follows: pricing and mix improvements from the Southeast Asia exit contributed ¥2.4 billion; volume recovery added ¥1.8 billion; the post-impairment depreciation reduction added ¥2.0 billion; and raw material cost headwinds subtracted ¥0.6 billion. Strip out the depreciation tailwind and the underlying operating improvement is still approximately ¥6.4 billion — a meaningful shift, though one that has not yet been stress-tested through a full commodity cycle.

## Balance Sheet Transformation: REVIC's Rescue in Numbers

The more dramatic financial story unfolded in the nine months ending December 2025. Between March 2025 and December 2025, cash and deposits rose from ¥13.5 billion to ¥58.0 billion — a ¥44.5 billion increase in a single three-quarter period. Net assets climbed from ¥16.2 billion to ¥45.7 billion. The capital adequacy ratio moved from 10.4 percent to 25.2 percent, crossing the threshold below which lenders and trading partners typically begin imposing punitive terms.

The source of this transformation was dual: the April 2025 issuance of Class C preferred shares to REVIC via third-party allotment, which injected ¥20 billion in equity and transferred 66.76 percent of voting rights to the state-backed turnaround fund; and the proceeds from asset divestitures, which generated a ¥23.7 billion gain on non-current asset sales in the nine months through December. Lenders — MUFG, Mizuho, and Sumitomo Mitsui Trust — separately approved up to ¥43 billion in debt forgiveness, though the drawn amount against that facility is not publicly itemised in the filings reviewed.

The nine-month extraordinary items illustrate why net income cannot be taken at face value. Of the ¥10.6 billion net income reported for the April–December 2025 period, ¥23.7 billion came from asset sale gains, offset by ¥12.4 billion in restructuring charges and a ¥0.9 billion FX gain, netting to ¥11.3 billion in extraordinary profit. Segment operating profit for the same period was ¥9.0 billion. The company is, in accounting terms, simultaneously more profitable and less valuable — selling its way to a cleaner income statement.

## Operating Quality vs. Accounting Quality

The honest distinction to make is between two different recovery stories running in parallel. The first is real: Unitika's Polymers segment generated ¥7.5 billion in operating profit in the first nine months of FY3/26, up 67 percent year-on-year, driven by nylon and polyester film growth in packaging and electronic materials. The EMBLEM-HG product line — a high-barrier nylon film used in food and pharmaceutical packaging — is growing. Performance Materials contributed ¥1.4 billion in operating profit, with glass fiber revenues for high-end mobile memory substrates growing "significantly" according to the Q3 commentary. Even the structurally challenged Fibers and Textiles segment turned marginally profitable at ¥50 million in operating profit, against a ¥560 million loss in the prior period.

The second story is accounting-driven: the ¥23.7 billion asset sale gain will not repeat in FY3/27 or FY3/28. The full-year net income guidance of ¥20 billion for FY3/26 rests heavily on gains from divestitures already contracted. Once those transactions close, the P&L loses its extraordinary tailwind, and the underlying ¥9.5 billion operating profit will have to carry the reported earnings line on its own.

## Forward Guidance and the Credibility of 9.3%

The February 2026 revision to full-year FY3/26 guidance sets revenue at ¥110 billion — a 13 percent decline from FY3/25 — and operating profit at ¥9.5 billion. That implies an OP margin of 8.6 percent, nearly double FY3/25's 4.7 percent. The revenue decline is structural: subsidiaries including Unitika Garment Technology, Unitika Spinning, and PT. Unitika Trading Indonesia have been deconsolidated, and the nonwovens business found a buyer in October 2025. Unitika is explicitly choosing to shrink in exchange for margin expansion.

The five-year target of ¥70 billion in revenue and ¥6.5 billion in operating profit — implying a 9.3 percent OP margin — is where scrutiny is warranted.

| Company | OP margin range (recent years) |
|---|---|
| Toray Industries | 5–7% |
| Teijin | ~5% |
| Unitika FY3/25 actual | 4.7% |
| Unitika FY3/26F | 8.6% |
| Unitika FY3/29 target | 9.3% |
| Specialty-only polymer peers | 12–15% |

A 9.3 percent target margin is achievable for a company that genuinely exits commodity manufacturing and retains only high-margin niches. But the comparison set matters. Toray, running a diversified specialty-materials portfolio at scale, manages 5–7 percent. Teijin, further along its own restructuring, hovers near 5 percent. Unitika's target implies it will outperform both larger peers — plausible if the retained businesses in semiconductor packaging films and glass fibers for mobile memory substrates can sustain the margins currently in evidence, but not yet verified by a full cycle. The 9M FY3/26 Polymers segment is running at a 17.8 percent OP margin on ¥42.5 billion of revenue, which is genuinely strong; sustaining that as the segment mix normalises post-divestiture is the key assumption.

## Who Is Not Being Paid

One number is unambiguous in its message to common shareholders: ¥0.00 per share in dividends, for the second consecutive fiscal year. REVIC, holding Class C preferred shares, receives ¥2.27 per share in preferred dividends — a modest coupon relative to its ¥20 billion equity injection, but a cash outflow that common holders are effectively subsidising through their own zero return. The priority structure is standard for a state-backed rescue: REVIC's capital comes first; common equity benefits only if and when the restructuring generates surplus above preferred obligations. With a 52-week range on the common stock of ¥140 to ¥4,380 and a trailing P/E of 45x against earnings heavily inflated by one-time asset gains, the equity market is currently pricing in successful execution of the five-year plan. That is a large bet on a company that has not yet delivered a clean, gain-free profitable year.
